analysis.one_liner: Guarantees Medicare-style government health coverage to every child born after 2006, funded by premiums collected through tax returns.
analysis.headline: The bill to automatically cover every child born after 2006 never received a committee vote; it sat in a House subcommittee until the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new program, MediKids, that automatically enrolls every child born after December 31, 2006 in government health coverage modeled on Medicare, lasting until age 23. Benefits would include everything Medicare covers, all required Medicaid benefits for children, prescription drugs, and reduced or zero cost-sharing for low-income families. Families with a covered child would pay a monthly premium through their tax return, capped at 5% of income, with very low-income families exempted. The bill also directs the Treasury to propose progressive tax changes to fund the program as enrollment grows.
analysis.who_benefits: Children born after 2006 would be covered from birth without enrollment gaps, and the more than 9 million uninsured children cited in the bill's findings would gain a guaranteed safety net that follows them across state lines and through parents' job changes. Low-income families pay nothing or sharply reduced cost-sharing, and a refundable tax credit caps a family's out-of-pocket cost-sharing at 5% of income.

how_it_helps.text: Every child born after December 31, 2006 would be deemed enrolled at birth in a Medicare-modeled program, with coverage that persists automatically when a family loses job-based insurance [S2] [S3].

The benefit package would include Medicare's core benefits, all mandatory Medicaid children's benefits including early screening and treatment, and prescription drugs at least equal to the 2005 federal employee standard option [S2] [S3].

Children in families below 150% of poverty would pay no cost-sharing, and cost-sharing would be cut 75% for families up to 200% of poverty and 50% up to 300%, with a refundable credit capping any family's cost-sharing at 5% of income [S3].
Families could keep private coverage or Medicaid/SCHIP with no premium owed, so MediKids acts as a default safety net rather than forcing families off existing coverage [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Families with covered children would pay monthly MediKids premiums through their tax returns, capped at 5% of adjusted gross income and waived entirely for very low-income families (exempt up to roughly $19,000-$34,000 of income depending on family size). The Treasury's general fund would cover costs before premiums arrive, and the bill directs Treasury to propose progressive tax increases to finance the program as enrollment grows.

drawbacks.text: The premium is a new tax-like payment on families with covered children, collected through the tax code; a middle-income family would owe up to 5% of its income even though the bill leaves the long-term funding design to a future Treasury report on 'progressive tax changes' [S3].

The benefit package, payment rates, and enrollment rules would largely be specified by the HHS Secretary rather than written into law, leaving future secretaries substantial discretion over what children actually receive [S3].

Payments to doctors and hospitals would follow Medicare-style reimbursement, which generally pays less than private insurance, and providers could not bill enrollees beyond Medicare's limits — an honest cost for supporters to acknowledge, since it could affect provider participation [S3].

Because eligibility expands gradually by age cohort, the program would take years to reach universal coverage and would run alongside, rather than replace, the existing patchwork of employer plans, Medicaid, and SCHIP [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and concrete: no child would ever be uninsured for lack of a safety net, and low-income families would be protected from medical bills entirely. The main costs are a new family premium (capped and waived for the poor) and an unfinished long-term financing plan that Congress would have to fill in later. The gradual phase-in means the biggest gains accrue to future cohorts of children, not to the millions uninsured at enactment. On balance the design is careful about cost-sharing and choice, but its financing rests on a promise of future progressive taxes that the bill itself does not enact.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to a Ways and Means health subcommittee in July 2005, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the MediKids Health Insurance Act on June 23, 2005, with 34 original cosponsors [S3] [S5].
The bill was referred the same day to the Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee, splitting jurisdiction over its financing and benefits provisions [S5].

On July 1, 2005 it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health, and the record shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — for the rest of the 109th Congress [S1] [S5].
All 55 cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent; no Republican signed on, in a Congress where Republicans controlled the House and its committees [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers kept the children's insurance market without a public default competitor, and employers faced no new payroll-side obligation. The roughly 9 million children uninsured at the time gained nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers; uninsured children gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: All 55 cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent, and the bill received no action from the Republican-controlled committees that held jurisdiction; no Republican ever signed on [S4] [S5].

industries.note: Every child born after 2006 would default into a public Medicare-like plan at birth, so insurers would lose those customers unless they could demonstrate equivalent coverage; the program also creates a permanent public fallback whenever a family loses private insurance. Their interest in the bill's defeat ran against the goal of guaranteed children's coverage [S3].

Providers would gain millions of currently uninsured children as paying patients, but reimbursement would follow Medicare-style payment rates and Medicare billing limits, which generally pay less than private insurance [S3].
The program must cover prescription drugs at least equal to the generous 2005 federal employee standard option, adding a large insured pediatric population that previously went without coverage [S3].
